'''Stephen James Lippard''' (born October 12, 1940) is the [[Arthur Amos Noyes]] Emeritus Professor of Chemistry at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].  He is considered one of the founders of [[bioinorganic chemistry]],<ref name="Halford"/> studying the interactions of nonliving substances such as metals with biological systems.<ref name="Franklin">{{cite web|title=Stephen J. Lippard|url=https://www.fi.edu/laureates/stephen-j-lippard|website=The Franklin Institute|access-date=24 May 2017|date=2014-10-27}}</ref>
He is also considered a founder of [[metalloneurochemistry]], the study of metal ions and their effects in the brain and nervous system.<ref name="Delaware">{{cite web|title='Metals for Life' Symposium to honor 2015 Benjamin Franklin Laureate in Chemistry|website=University of Delaware|date=April 10, 2015|url=http://www1.udel.edu/udaily/2015/apr/franklin-laureate-041015.html|access-date=24 March 2017}}</ref>   He has done pioneering work in understanding protein structure and synthesis, the enzymatic functions of [[methane monooxygenase]] (MMO), and the mechanisms of [[cisplatin]] anticancer drugs.<ref name="Franklin"/> His work has applications for the treatment of cancer,<ref name="Delaware"/> for bioremediation of the environment,<ref name="Koukkou"/> and for the development of synthetic [[methanol]]-based fuels.<ref name="Franklin"/>

==Education==
Lippard was born in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, where he graduated from [[Taylor Allderdice High School]] in 1958. He earned his bachelor's degree from [[Haverford College]] in 1962.<ref name="LRGBio"/>  Originally interested in attending medical school, a talk on [[medicinal chemistry]] by visiting chemist [[Francis Patrick Dwyer|Francis P.J. Dwyer]] inspired Lippard to focus on [[inorganic chemistry]] for his Ph.D.<ref name="Franklin"/>  Lippard worked with [[F. Albert Cotton]] at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] on [[rhenium]] [[Transition metal oxo complex|oxo complexes]] and [[Cluster chemistry|clusters]]. He completed the thesis ''Chemistry of the bromorhenates'', receiving his Ph.D. from MIT in 1965.<ref name="LRGBio"/><ref name="Tree">{{cite web|title=Stephen James Lippard|url=https://academictree.org/chemistry/peopleinfo.php?pid=52409|website=Chemistry Tree|access-date=23 March 2017}}</ref><ref name="Halford">{{cite journal|last1=Halford|first1=Bethany|title=Trailblazer And Mentor|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=March 17, 2014|volume=92|issue=11|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/92/i11/Trailblazer-Mentor.html|access-date=24 March 2017}}</ref><ref name="Cotton">{{cite journal|last1=Morrissey|first1=Susan |title=F. Albert Cotton Dies|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=February 26, 2007|volume=85|issue=9|page=11|url=https://pubs.acs.org/cen/news/85/i09/8509notw5.html}}</ref>

==Career==
Lippard joined the faculty of [[Columbia University]] in 1966 as an assistant professor. He was promoted to associate professor with tenure in 1969 and full Professor in 1972.<ref name="Nucleus"/>

In 1983, Lippard returned to MIT as a professor of chemistry.<ref name="Nucleus"/> He has held the Arthur Amos Noyes Professorship of Chemistry at MIT since 1989.<ref name="Leopoldina">{{cite web|title=Curriculum Vitae Professor Dr. Stephen J. Lippard|url=http://www.leopoldina.org/fileadmin/redaktion/Mitglieder/CV_Lippard_Stephen_EN.pdf|website=Leopoldina|access-date=23 March 2017}}</ref>  
He and his wife Judy were housemasters at MIT's MacGregor House from 1991 to 1995.<ref name="Lane">{{cite news|last1=Lane|first1=Jennifer|title=MacGregor, Burton Housmasters to Leave|url=http://tech.mit.edu/V115/N10/hmaster.10n.html|access-date=26 May 2017|work=The Tech|date=March 10, 1995}}</ref>
Lippard served as the head of the MIT chemistry department from 1995 to 2005.<ref name="LRGBio"/> He is recognized for his scientific work and for his work with students, having mentored more than 100 PhDs.<ref name="ACS2013"/><ref name="Halford"/><ref name="Trafton"/> His students are active in a wide range of areas, in part because "He delivers a strong message that you need to go to the frontier of science and pick interesting problems."<ref name="Halford"/> Forty percent of his graduate students have been women, who he gives "high-risk, high-reward projects".<ref name="Halford"/>

Lippard has co-authored over 900 scholarly and professional articles,<ref name="LRGBio"/> and co-authored the textbook ''Principles of Bioinorganic Chemistry'' (1994) with [[Jeremy Berg]].<ref name="Berg">{{cite book|editor-last1=Lippard|editor-first1=Stephen J.|editor-last2=Berg|editor-first2=Jeremy M.|title=Principles of bioinorganic chemistry|date=1994|publisher=University Science Books|location=Mill Valley, Calif.|isbn=978-0935702729}}</ref>  He edited the book series ''Progress in Inorganic Chemistry'' from Volume 11 to 40.<ref name="Wiley">{{cite book|title=Progress in Inorganic Chemistry (Series)|volume=55|doi=10.1002/SERIES2229|year=2007|isbn=9780470144428|editor1-last=Karlin|editor1-first=Kenneth D}}</ref> He was an Associate Editor of the journal ''Inorganic Chemistry'' from 1983 to 1989,<ref name="Halford"/> and an Associate Editor of the ''[[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]'' from 1989 to 2013,<ref name="Halford"/><ref name="LRGBio"/> as well as serving on the editorial boards of numerous other journals.<ref name="Nucleus">{{cite journal|title=Biography|journal=The Nucleus|date=March 2002|volume=LXXX|issue=7|pages=4, 6|url=http://www.nesacs.org/pub_nucleus/2002/Mar02.pdf}}</ref>

==Research==
Lippard's research activities are at the interface of biology and inorganic chemistry. Lippard focuses on understanding the physical and structural properties of metal complexes, their synthesis and reactions, and the involvement of metal ions in biological systems.<ref name="CSULB">{{cite web|title=MIT's Lippard to Present Allergan Distinguished Lecture March 23|url=http://web.csulb.edu/misc/inside/2011/03/15/mit-chemistry-professor-stephen-j-lippard-to-present-allergan-distinguished-lecture/|website=Inside CSULB|date=March 15, 2011}}</ref><ref name="Bertini"/><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lippard|first1=Stephen J.|title=The inorganic side of chemical biology|journal=Nature Chemical Biology|date=October 2006|volume=2|issue=10|pages=504–507|doi=10.1038/nchembio1006-504|pmid=16983380|s2cid=45014853}}</ref> The formation and breaking of molecular bonds underlie many biochemical transformations. Purely inorganic substances such as iron are often required in essential organic reactions, e.g. oxygen binding in the hemoglobin family.  Lippard attempts to better understand the role of metal complexes in the physiology and pathology of existing biological systems, and to identify possible applications of metal ions in medical treatment.<ref name="Bertini">{{cite book|editor-last1=Bertini|editor-first1=Ivano|editor-last2=Gray|editor-first2=Harry B.|editor-last3=Lippard|editor-first3=Stephen J.|editor-last4=Valentine|editor-first4=Joan Selverstone|title=Bioinorganic chemistry|date=1994|publisher=Univ. Science Books|location=Mill Valley, Calif.|isbn=978-0-935702-57-6|last1=Lippard|first1=Stephen J.|chapter=Metals in Medicine|pages=505–583|chapter-url=http://authors.library.caltech.edu/25052/1/BioinCh.pdf|access-date=25 May 2017}}</ref>

He has made major contributions in a number of areas, including the development of [[platinum-based anticancer drugs]] such as the [[cisplatin]] family.<ref name="Johnstone">{{cite journal|last1=Johnstone|first1=Timothy C.|last2=Suntharalingam|first2=Kogularamanan|last3=Lippard|first3=Stephen J.|title=The Next Generation of Platinum Drugs: Targeted Pt(II) Agents, Nanoparticle Delivery, and Pt(IV) Prodrugs|journal=Chemical Reviews|date=9 March 2016|volume=116|issue=5|pages=3436–3486|doi=10.1021/acs.chemrev.5b00597|pmc=4792284|pmid=26865551 |bibcode=2016ChRv..116.3436J }}</ref>  
Another area of interest is the structure and function of [[methane]] and [[enzymes]] that consume greenhouse gas hydrocarbons.<ref name="Wang">{{cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Weixue|last2=Iacob|first2=Roxana E.|last3=Luoh|first3=Rebecca P.|last4=Engen|first4=John R.|last5=Lippard|first5=Stephen J.|title=Electron Transfer Control in Soluble Methane Monooxygenase|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|date=9 July 2014|volume=136|issue=27|pages=9754–9762|doi=10.1021/ja504688z|pmc=4105053|pmid=24937475|bibcode=2014JAChS.136.9754W }}</ref>
In metalloneurochemistry, he studies the molecular activity of metal ions in the brain and develops optical and MRI sensors for binding, tracking, and measuring metal ions as they interact with neurotransmitters and other biological signaling agents.<ref name="Grantome">{{cite journal|last1=Lippard|first1=Stephen J.|title=Investigation of Zinc Neurochemistry by Optical Sensing and MRI|url=http://grantome.com/grant/NIH/R01-GM065519-12|journal=Grantome|access-date=25 March 2017}}</ref><ref name="MIT Chemistry"/>

===Cisplatin===
[[File:Cisplatin-3D-balls.png | thumb|right | Cisplatin]]
[[Cisplatin]] is one of the most frequently used [[chemotherapy]] medications for many forms of cancer.  It was discovered in the 1960s by [[Barnett Rosenberg]], but its mechanism of action was not understood.<ref name="Brown"/><ref name="Rosenberg">{{Cite journal | last1 = Rosenberg | first1 = B. | last2 = Van Camp | first2 = L. | last3 = Krigas | first3 = T. | doi = 10.1038/205698a0 | title = Inhibition of Cell Division in Escherichia coli by Electrolysis Products from a Platinum Electrode | journal = Nature | volume = 205 | issue = 4972 | pages = 698–9 | year = 1965 | pmid =  14287410| bibcode = 1965Natur.205..698R | s2cid = 9543916 }}</ref>

Early work in Lippard's lab on the interaction of [[metal complexes]] with [[nucleic acids]] led to the discovery of the first [[DNA-binding metallo-intercalators|metallo-intercalators]] and eventually to the understanding of the mechanisms of cisplatin. 
Lippard and his students examined sequences of DNA and RNA and incorporated  sulfur atoms into the sugar-phosphate backbone, where they selectively bound mercury or platinum complexes to specific positions. Karen Jennette's discovery that sterically encumbered platinum complexes were more successful in binding to sulfur atoms in tRNA than mercury salts led researchers to propose that the platinum complexes intercalated between the double-stranded RNA's base pairs.<ref name="Life"/> It was the first experimental demonstration to show a metal complex binding to DNA by intercalation: platinum terpyridine complexes inserted between the DNA base pairs and unwound the double helix.<ref name="Howell">{{cite book|editor-last1=Howell|editor-first1=Stephen B.|title=Platinum and other metal coordination compounds in cancer chemotherapy|date=1991|publisher=Plenum Press|location=New York|isbn=9780306440274|last=Lippard|first=Stephen J.|chapter=Platinum DNA Chemistry|pages=1–12|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aKrzBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA1|access-date=25 May 2017}}</ref>  Using fiber X-ray diffraction, Peter Bond and others were able to display the intercalated platinum complex and to confirm predictions that the spacing of intercalators in DNA base pairs would follow the neighbor exclusion rule.<ref name="Life">{{cite journal|last1=Lippard|first1=Stephen J.|title=The Life Of A Professor|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=March 17, 2014|volume=92|issue=11|pages=14–18|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/92/i11/Life-Professor.html|access-date=25 May 2017|doi=10.1021/cen-09211-cover2|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name="Jennette">{{cite journal|last1=Jennette|first1=KW|last2=Lippard|first2=SJ|last3=Vassiliades|first3=GA|last4=Bauer|first4=WR|title=Metallointercalation reagents. 2-hydroxyethanethiolato(2,2',2'-terpyridine)-platinum(II) monocation binds strongly to DNA by intercalation.|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|date=October 1974|volume=71|issue=10|pages=3839–43|pmid=4530265|doi=10.1073/pnas.71.10.3839|pmc=434279|bibcode=1974PNAS...71.3839J|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Bond">{{cite journal|last1=Bond|first1=PJ|last2=Langridge|first2=R|last3=Jennette|first3=KW|last4=Lippard|first4=SJ|title=X-ray fiber diffraction evidence for neighbor exclusion binding of a platinum metallointercalation reagent to DNA.|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|date=December 1975|volume=72|issue=12|pages=4825–9|pmid=1061071|doi=10.1073/pnas.72.12.4825|pmc=388824|bibcode=1975PNAS...72.4825B|doi-access=free}}</ref>

This established the groundwork for subsequent work on intercalative binding.<ref name="Howell"/> [[Jacqueline Barton]] and others have used [[Electron microscope|electron micrography]] to show that the covalent binding of platinum complexes changes the supercoiling of the DNA, "bending and unwinding" the double helix.
<ref name="Johnstone"/><ref name="Cohen">{{cite journal|last1=Cohen|first1=GL|last2=Bauer|first2=WR|last3=Barton|first3=JK|last4=Lippard|first4=SJ|title=Binding of cis- and trans-dichlorodiammineplatinum(II) to DNA: evidence for unwinding and shortening of the double helix.|journal=Science|date=9 March 1979|volume=203|issue=4384|pages=1014–6|pmid=370979|doi=10.1126/science.370979|bibcode=1979Sci...203.1014C}}</ref><ref name="Zeglis">{{cite journal|last1=Zeglis|first1=Brian M.|last2=Pierre|first2=Valerie C.|last3=Barton|first3=Jacqueline K.|title=Metallo-intercalators and metallo-insertors|journal=Chemical Communications|date=2007|issue=44|pages=4565–79|doi=10.1039/b710949k|pmc=2790054|pmid=17989802|url=http://authors.library.caltech.edu/9287/1/ZEGcc07.pdf}}</ref>
Further experiments have explored the mechanisms through which platinum drugs bind their biological targets and led to insights into their anticancer activity. Important results include the identification of an intrastrand d(pGpG) cross-link as the major adduct on platinated single-stranded DNA,<ref name="Sherman">{{cite journal|last1=Sherman|first1=Suzanne E.|last2=Lippard|first2=Stephen J.|title=Structural aspects of platinum anticancer drug interactions with DNA|journal=Chemical Reviews|date=October 1987|volume=87|issue=5|pages=1153–1181|doi=10.1021/cr00081a013}}</ref> identification of the major adduct on double-stranded DNA, the binding of high-mobility-group proteins to platinated DNA cross-links.<ref name="Life"/><ref name="MIT Chemistry">{{cite web|title=MIT Chemistry Directory Stephen J. Lippard Arthur Amos Noyes Professor|url=http://chemistry.mit.edu/people/lippard-stephen|website=MIT Chemistry|access-date=25 March 2017}}</ref> Using X-ray crystallography and other techniques,  Lippard and his coworkers have examined the mechanisms involved in binding cisplatin to DNA fragments, to better understand how cisplatin invades tumor cells and interferes with their activity.<ref name="Franklin"/>  The interaction of Cisplatin and DNA results in the formation of DNA-DNA interstrand and intrastrand crosslinks which block DNA replication and transcription mechanisms.<ref name="Brown">{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=J. M.|last2=Mehta|first2=M.P.|last3=Nieder|first3=Carsten|title=Multimodal concepts for integration of cytotoxic drugs with 73 tables|date=2006|publisher=Springer|location=Berlin|isbn=9783540256557|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dTRNAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA94|access-date=25 May 2017}}</ref>
As well as the intrastrand cross links created by cisplatin, monofunctional metal complexes may suggest possible cancer treatments.<ref name="Zhang">{{cite journal|last1=Zhang|first1=Christiana Xin|last2=Lippard|first2=Stephen J|title=New metal complexes as potential therapeutics|journal=Current Opinion in Chemical Biology|date=August 2003|volume=7|issue=4|pages=481–489|doi=10.1016/S1367-5931(03)00081-4|pmid=12941423 |bibcode=2003COCB....7..481Z }}</ref><ref name="Park">{{cite journal|last1=Park|first1=Ga Young|last2=Wilson|first2=Justin J.|last3=Song|first3=Ying|last4=Lippard|first4=Stephen J.|title=Phenanthriplatin, a monofunctional DNA-binding platinum anticancer drug candidate with unusual potency and cellular activity profile|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date=24 July 2012|volume=109|issue=30|pages=11987–11992|doi=10.1073/pnas.1207670109|pmid=22773807|pmc=3409760|bibcode=2012PNAS..10911987P|doi-access=free}}</ref>

A related line of research in Lippard's laboratory involves platinum blues. Jacqueline Barton was the first person to synthesize and structurally characterize a crystalline platinum blue, pyridone blue. Since then, extensive research has been done on the structure, properties, and reactions of such complexes.<ref name="Life"/><ref name="Matsumoto">{{cite book|editor-last1=Lippert|editor-first1=Bernhard|last=Matsumoto|first=Kazuko|title=Cisplatin : chemistry and biochemistry of a leading anticancer drug|date=1999|publisher=Verlag Helvetica Chimica Acta|location=Zürich|isbn=9783906390208|chapter=Inorganic and organometallic chemistry of cisplatin-derived diplatinum(III) complexes|pages=456–458|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Yii3zZRSb7cC&pg=PA456|access-date=25 May 2017}}</ref><ref name="Barton">{{cite journal|last1=Barton|first1=J. K.|last2=Rabinowitz|first2=H. N.|last3=Szalda|first3=D. J.|last4=Lippard|first4=S. J.|title=Synthesis and crystal structure of cis-diammineplatinum .alpha.-pyridone blue|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|date=April 1977|volume=99|issue=8|pages=2827–2829|doi=10.1021/ja00450a085|bibcode=1977JAChS..99.2827B }}</ref>

===Methane monooxygenases===
[[File:1yew opm.png | thumb|right | Particulate methane monooxygenase]]
Members of the Lippard laboratory studying macromolecular crystallography have explored the structure,  mechanisms and activity of bacterial multicomponent monooxygenases.<ref name="MIT Chemistry"/><ref name="Tinberg">{{cite journal|last1=Tinberg|first1=Christine E.|last2=Lippard|first2=Stephen J.|title=Dioxygen Activation in Soluble Methane Monooxygenase|journal=Accounts of Chemical Research|date=19 April 2011|volume=44|issue=4|pages=280–288|doi=10.1021/ar1001473|pmid=21391602|pmc=3079780}}</ref>
Methane monooxygenases are enzymes that occur in bacteria called methanotrophs.
The primary function of this enzyme is the [[hydroxylation]] of methane to methanol as the first step in [[Methanotroph|methane metabolism]].

[[Amy Rosenzweig]] determined the protein x-ray structure of the soluble form of [[methane monooxygenase]] (MMO) as Lippard's graduate student.<ref name="Halford"/><ref name="Structure">{{cite journal|last1=Rosenzweig|first1=Amy C.|last2=Frederick|first2=Christin A.|last3=Lippard|first3=Stephen J.|last4=Nordlund|first4=Pär|title=Crystal structure of a bacterial non-haem iron hydroxylase that catalyses the biological oxidation of methane|journal=Nature|date=9 December 1993|volume=366|issue=6455|pages=537–543|doi=10.1038/366537a0|pmid=8255292|bibcode=1993Natur.366..537R|s2cid=4237249}}</ref> Lippard has used X-ray diffraction and a variety of other methods to study such compounds, greatly expanding our understanding of their structure and function. MMO is vital to Earth's carbon cycle, and knowledge of its structure may help to develop clean technologies for methanol-based fuels.<ref name="Franklin"/> Methane monoxygenases may also be useful for [[bioremediation]].<ref name="Koukkou">{{cite book|last1=Koukkou|first1=Anna-Irini|title=Microbial bioremediation of non-metals : current research|date=2011|publisher=Caister Academic Press|location=Norfolk|isbn=9781904455837|pages=217–232|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=txqpeZdx6eAC&pg=PA219|access-date=26 May 2017}}</ref>

===Iron complexes===
Lippard and his students have also studied the synthesis of diiron complexes such as diiron hydroxylase to better understand the activities of metal atoms in biological molecules.  They have developed model compounds for carboxylate-bridged diiron metalloenzymes which can be compared with corresponding biological forms.  They have synthesized analogues of the diiron carboxylate cores of MMO and related carboxylate-bridged diiron proteins such as the dioxygen transporter [[hemerythrin]].<ref name="Que">{{cite book|last1=Que|first1=Lawrence|last2=True|first2=Anne E.|title=Dinuclear Iron- and Manganese-Oxo Sites in Biology|journal=Progress in Inorganic Chemistry: Bioinorganic Chemistry|date=1990|volume=38|pages=97–200|doi=10.1002/9780470166390.ch3|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AbjulHMK9IAC&pg=PA99|access-date=24 March 2017|isbn=9780470166963|series=Progress in Inorganic Chemistry}}</ref><ref name="MIT Chemistry"/><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Friesner | first1 = R. A. | last2 = Baik | first2 = M.-H. | last3 = Gherman | first3 = B. F. | last4 = Guallar | first4 = V. | last5 = Wirstam | first5 = M. | last6 = Murphy | first6 = R. B. | last7 = Lippard | first7 = S. J. | year = 2003 | title = How iron-containing proteins control dioxygen chemistry: a detailed atomic level description via accurate quantum chemical and mixed quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics calculations | journal = Coord. Chem. Rev. | volume = 238–239 | pages = 267–290 | doi = 10.1016/S0010-8545(02)00284-9 }}</ref> In 2010, Lippard received the Ronald Breslow Award for his work on nonheme iron proteins.<ref name="Breslow">{{cite journal|last1=Baum|first1=Rudy M.|title=Ronald Breslow Award For Achievement In Biomimetic Chemistry Sponsored by the Ronald Breslow Award Endowment|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=February 15, 2010|volume=88|issue=7|page=61|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/88/i7/Ronald-Breslow-Award-Achievement-Biomimetic.html?type=paidArticleContent|access-date=26 May 2017}}</ref>

Also exciting was the synthesis of a "molecular ferric wheel" by Kingsley Taft, the first wheel structure to be observed in self-assembled polymetallic chemistry.<ref name="Baum">{{cite journal|last1=Baum|first1=Rudy|title="Ferric wheel" molecule characterized at MIT|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=24 December 1990|volume=68|issue=52|pages=22|doi=10.1021/cen-v068n052.p022}}</ref><ref name="Kovac">{{cite book|editor-last1=Kovac|editor-first1=Jeffrey|editor-last2=Weisberg|editor-first2=Michael|title=Roald Hoffmann on the philosophy, art, and science of chemistry|date=2012|publisher=Oxford University Press|location=New York|isbn=978-0199755905|pages=133–137|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=i1RpAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA133|access-date=26 May 2017}}</ref><ref name="Taft">{{cite journal|last1=Taft|first1=Kingsley L.|last2=Lippard|first2=Stephen J.|title=Synthesis and structure of [Fe(OMe)2(O2CCH2Cl)]10: a molecular ferric wheel|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|date=December 1990|volume=112|issue=26|pages=9629–9630|doi=10.1021/ja00182a027|bibcode=1990JAChS.112.9629T }}</ref>
<ref name="Kingsley">{{cite journal|last1=Taft|first1=Kingsley L.|last2=Delfs|first2=Christopher D.|last3=Papaefthymiou|first3=Georgia C.|last4=Foner|first4=Simon|last5=Gatteschi|first5=Dante|last6=Lippard|first6=Stephen J.|title=[Fe(OMe)2(O2CCH2Cl)]10, a Molecular Ferric Wheel|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|date=February 1994|volume=116|issue=3|pages=823–832|doi=10.1021/ja00082a001|bibcode=1994JAChS.116..823T }}</ref>
A nearly perfect circle containing ten ferric ions, the structure spontaneously assembled in methanolic solutions of diiron(III) oxo complexes, which were being studied to better understand polyiron oxo protein cores like those of hemerythrin.<ref name="Baum"/><ref name="Stover">{{cite news|last1=Stover|first1=Dawn|title=Science Newsfront: Ferric Wheel|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zAIugfGhlj8C&pg=PA21|access-date=26 May 2017|work=Popular Science|page=21|date=May 1991}}</ref> Although no particular use is known for the ferric wheel, it and subsequent ring-shaped homometallic molecular clusters are of interest as a subclass of molecular magnets.<ref name="Winpenny">{{cite book|last1=Winpenny|first1=Richard|title=Molecular cluster magnets|date=2012|publisher=World Scientific Publishing|location=Singapore|isbn=978-9814322942|pages=192–193|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LUMVs491tZgC&pg=PA192|access-date=26 May 2017}}</ref>  Another novel complex was a "ferric triple-decker", containing three parallel triangular iron units and a triple bridge of six citrate ligands.<ref name="Bino">{{cite journal|last1=Bino|first1=Avi|last2=Shweky|first2=Itzhak|last3=Cohen|first3=Shmuel|last4=Bauminger|first4=Erika R.|last5=Lippard|first5=Stephen J.|title=A Novel Nonairon(III) Citrate Complex: A "Ferric Triple-Decker"|journal=Inorganic Chemistry|date=October 1998|volume=37|issue=20|pages=5168–5172|doi=10.1021/ic9715658 |bibcode=1998InCh...37.5168B }}</ref>

===Metalloneurochemistry===
Lippard is considered a founder of [[metalloneurochemistry]],<ref name="Delaware"/> the study of metal ions at the molecular level as they affect the brain and the nervous system.<ref name="Burdette">{{cite journal|last1=Burdette|first1=S. C.|last2=Lippard|first2=S. J.|title=Meeting of the minds: Metalloneurochemistry|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date=24 March 2003|volume=100|issue=7|pages=3605–3610|doi=10.1073/pnas.0637711100|pmid=12655069|pmc=152969|doi-access=free}}</ref> Working at the interface of inorganic chemistry and neuroscience, he has devised fluorescent imaging agents for studying mobile zinc and nitric oxide and their effects on neurotransmission and other forms of biological signaling.<ref name="Dean">{{cite journal|last1=Dean|first1=Kevin M.|last2=Qin|first2=Yan|last3=Palmer|first3=Amy E.|title=Visualizing metal ions in cells: An overview of analytical techniques, approaches, and probes|journal=Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Molecular Cell Research|date=September 2012|volume=1823|issue=9|pages=1406–1415|doi=10.1016/j.bbamcr.2012.04.001|pmid=22521452|pmc=3408866}}</ref><ref name="Goldberg">{{cite journal|last1=Goldberg|first1=Jacob M.|last2=Loas|first2=Andrei|last3=Lippard|first3=Stephen J.|title=Metalloneurochemistry and the Pierian Spring: 'Shallow Draughts Intoxicate the Brain'|journal=Israel Journal of Chemistry|date=October 2016|volume=56|issue=9–10|pages=791–802|doi=10.1002/ijch.201600034|pmc=5300766|pmid=28190893}}</ref><ref name="MIT Chemistry"/>

==Companies==
In 2011 Lippard founded Blend Therapeutics with [[Omid Cameron Farokhzad]] and [[Robert Langer]], in Watertown, Massachusetts.<ref name="Tomczyk">{{cite book|last1=Tomczyk|first1=Michael|title=Nanoinnovation : What Every Manager Needs to Know.|date=2012|publisher=Wiley & Sons, Incorporated, John|isbn=978-3527326723|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xtGRBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA255|access-date=24 March 2017}}</ref> 
Blend focused on developing anti-cancer medicines for treatment of solid tumor cancers,<ref name="Morris"/> with the goal of targeting cancerous tissue and leaving healthy cells alone.<ref name="Fidler2015"/> Its proprietary drug candidates included BTP-114, a cisplatin prodrug, and BTP-277, a targeting ligand designed to bond selectively to tumor cells.<ref name="Morris">{{cite web|last1=Morris|first1=Kathryn|title=BTP-277 has evolved to become PEN-221, embodying the miniaturized biologic drug conjugate targeting the somatostatin receptor, but no longer encapsulated in a nanoparticle.|url=http://www.tarveda.com/pr_04212015_2.html|access-date=24 March 2017|work=Tarveda|date=April 21, 2015}}</ref><ref name="Fidler2015">{{cite news|last1=Fidler|first1=Ben|title=With $21M, Retooled Blend Whips up Mini-Smart Bombs For Cancer|journal=Xconomy|date=January 7, 2015 |url=http://www.xconomy.com/boston/2015/01/07/with-21m-retooled-blend-whips-up-mini-smart-bombs-for-cancer/|access-date=24 March 2017}}</ref> As of 2016, Blend split off into two separate companies: Tarveda and Placon, to follow these two approaches.<ref name="Fidler2016"/>

Placon Therapeutics is developing platinum-based cancer therapies. These  include BTP-114, the first clinical candidate to use an albumin-conjugating, platinum-prodrug platform, based on Lippard's work. BTP-114 has been cleared for Phase 1 cancer-treatment clinical trials by the [[Food and Drug Administration]] (FDA).{{Citation needed|date=May 2026}}

Tarveda Therapeutics is developing BTP-277 (renamed PEN-221) and other Pentarins, a proprietary class of therapeutics which use peptide ligands to carry a target drug to tumor cells.<ref name="Fidler2016">{{cite news|last1=Fidler|first1=Ben|title=Blend Rebrands as Tarveda, Raises $38M, and Spins Out Cancer Drug|journal=Xconomy|date=January 27, 2016|url=http://www.xconomy.com/boston/2016/01/27/blend-rebrands-as-tarveda-raises-38m-and-spins-out-cancer-drug/#|access-date=24 March 2017}}</ref> Pentarins are nanoparticle drugs, similar to [[antibody-drug conjugates]] but smaller, that have been described as "mini-smart bombs". They are believed to be capable of penetrating dense tumor-based cancers.<ref name="Fidler2015"/>

==Honors and awards==
Lippard has been elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]], the [[National Institute of Medicine]], the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]],<ref name="Nucleus"/> and the [[American Philosophical Society]].<ref name="Philosophical">{{cite news|title=Four MIT professors elected to the American Philosophical Society|url=http://tagteam.harvard.edu/hub_feeds/2405/feed_items/2175174|access-date=23 March 2017|work=MIT News|date=2016-05-14}}</ref>  He is an honorary member of the [[Royal Irish Academy]] (2002),<ref name="RIA2002">{{cite web|title=Stephen J. Lippard|url=https://www.ria.ie/stephen-j-lippard|website=Royal Irish Academy|access-date=23 March 2017|date=2015-10-19}}</ref> the [[Italian Chemical Society]] (1996), and the German National Academy of Sciences ([[German Academy of Sciences Leopoldina|Leopoldina]]) (2004), and is an external scientific member of the [[Max-Planck Institute]] (1996) in Germany.<ref name="MPI">{{cite web|title=Our roots|url=https://cec.mpg.de/1/institute/history/|website=MPI für Chemische Energiekonversion|access-date=24 March 2017}}</ref>

He has received honorary [[Doctorate of Science]] degrees from [[Haverford College]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.haverford.edu/news/stories/23491/51 |title=As Part Of Its Major Campaign Kick-Off, Haverford College Honors Leaders In Business, Medicine, Higher Education And Community Service |date=3 December 2000 |publisher=[[Haverford College]] |access-date=2013-11-06}}</ref> [[Texas A&M University]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://web.mit.edu/annualreports/pres95/14.03.html |title=MIT Reports to the President 1994-95 |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |access-date=2013-11-06}}</ref> and the [[University of South Carolina]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sc.edu/news/newsarticle_print.php?nid=928 |title=Bernanke, Robinson to address graduates |publisher=[[University of South Carolina]] |date=2010-02-01 |access-date=2013-11-06}}</ref> and an honorary [[Doctorate]] degree from [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://chemistry.mit.edu/chemistry-news/lippard-awarded-honorary-doctorate-from-the-hebrew-university-of-jerusalem/ |title=Lippard Awarded Honorary Doctorate from The Hebrew University of Jerusalem |publisher=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] |date=2018-06-13|access-date=2019-07-19}}</ref>

Lippard has received many awards throughout his career,<ref name="Nucleus"/> most notably the 2004 [[National Medal of Science]], the 2014 [[Priestley Medal]] of the American Chemical Society, its highest award,<ref name="Faiz">{{cite journal|last1=Faiz|first1=Jonathan Faiz|title=Stephen Lippard Awarded the Priestley Medal|journal=ChemistryViews|date=18 March 2014|url=http://www.chemistryviews.org/details/ezine/5836951/Stephen_Lippard_Awarded_the_Priestley_Medal.html|access-date=23 March 2017}}</ref> and the 2014 [[James Rhyne Killian|James R. Killian]] lectureship at MIT, given to one faculty member of the Institute per year.<ref name="Trafton">{{cite news|last1=Trafton|first1=Anne|title=Stephen Lippard wins faculty's Killian Award|url=http://chemistry.mit.edu/stephen-lippard-wins-faculty%E2%80%99s-killian-award|access-date=24 March 2017|work=MIT Department of Chemistry|date=May 16, 2013}}</ref> He is also the recipient of the [[Linus Pauling]] Medal,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://web.pdx.edu/~wamserc/Pauling2009/ |title=Pauling Award |publisher=[[Portland State University]] |date=2009-11-07 |access-date=2013-11-06}}</ref> [[Theodore W. Richards]] Medal,<ref name="NESACS">{{cite web|title=Theodore William Richards Medal for Conspicuous Achievement in Chemistry Recipients|url=http://www.nesacs.org/awards/richards-medal/awards_richards-medal_recipients.html|website=Northeastern Section of the American Chemical Society|access-date=24 March 2017|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305061948/http://www.nesacs.org/awards/richards-medal/awards_richards-medal_recipients.html|archive-date=5 March 2016}}</ref> and the [[William H. Nichols]] Medal.<ref name="Nichols">{{cite web|title=Nichols Medalists|url=http://www.newyorkacs.org/nicholsmedalists.html|website=New York Section, American Chemical Society|access-date=24 March 2017}}</ref> For his work in bioinorganic and biomimetic chemistry, Lippard received the [[Ronald Breslow]] Award<ref name="Biomimetic">{{cite web|title=Ronald Breslow Award for Achievement in Biomimetic Chemistry|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/ronald-breslow-award-for-achievement-in-biomimetic-chemistry.html|website=American Chemical Society|access-date=24 March 2017}}</ref> and the [[Alfred Bader]] Award<ref>{{cite web|url=http://portal.acs.org/portal/acs/corg/content?_nfpb=true&_pageLabel=PP_ARTICLEMAIN&node_id=1319&content_id=CTP_004490&use_sec=true&sec_url_var=region1&__uuid=446126fc-d987-402b-aa9b-f34832854527 |title=Alfred Bader Award in Bioinorganic or Bioorganic Chemistry |publisher=[[American Chemical Society]] |access-date=2013-11-06}}</ref> from the [[American Chemical Society]] (ACS).  For research in inorganic and organometallic chemistry, as well as his role as an educator, he was honored with ACS awards for Inorganic Chemistry<ref name="ACS1987">{{cite web|title=ACS Award in Inorganic Chemistry|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/acs-award-in-inorganic-chemistry.html|website=American Chemical Society|access-date=24 March 2017}}</ref> and for Distinguished Service in Inorganic Chemistry.<ref name="ACS1994">{{cite web|title=ACS Award for Distinguished Service in the Advancement of lnorganic Chemistry|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/acs-award-for-distinguished-service-in-the-advancement-of-lnorganic-chemistry.html|website=American Chemical Society|access-date=24 March 2017}}</ref> In 2015, Lippard won the Benjamin Franklin Medal in Chemistry bestowed by The Franklin Institute.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.fi.edu/laureates/stephen-j-lippard |title = Stephen J. Lippard|date = 2014-10-27}}</ref> In 2016, he received the F. A. Cotton Medal for excellence in chemical research<ref name="TAMU2016">{{cite web|title=MIT Chemist Stephen Lippard to Receive 2016 Cotton Medal|url=http://www.science.tamu.edu/news/story.php?story_ID=1544#.WNRCc461scg|website=Science Texas A&M University|date=February 18, 2016}}</ref><ref name="Linda">{{cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Linda|title=Stephen Lippard named Cotton Medalist|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=May 9, 2016|volume=94 Issue|issue=19|page=36|doi=10.1016/j.cej.2016.04.041|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/94/i19/Stephen-Lippard-named-Cotton-Medalist.html?type=paidArticleContent|url-access=subscription|doi-access=free}}</ref> and the [[Welch Award in Chemistry]] from the [[Robert A. Welch Foundation]].<ref name="Welch">{{cite news|title=Stephen Lippard wins 2016 Welch Award|url=https://news.mit.edu/2016/stephen-lippard-wins-welch-award-0913|access-date=25 May 2017|work=MIT News|date=September 13, 2016}}</ref> In 2017, he was chosen to receive the [[American Institute of Chemists Gold Medal]].<ref name="AICGOld">{{cite web|title=American Institute of Chemists Gold Medal|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/american-institute-of-chemists-gold-medal|publisher=[[Science History Institute]]|date=March 22, 2018}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Stephen Lippard married Judith Ann Drezner in 1964.<ref name="Judith"/> They have two sons, Josh and Alex, a daughter-in-law Sandra, and twin granddaughters, Lucy and Annie.<ref name="ACS2013">{{cite web|title=American Chemical Society's highest honor goes to Stephen J. Lippard, Ph.D.|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/pressroom/newsreleases/2013/june/american-chemical-societys-highest-honor-goes-to-stephen-j-lippard-phd.html|website=American Chemical Society|access-date=June 10, 2013}}</ref> Judy Lippard died on September 9, 2013.<ref name="Judith">{{cite web|url=http://www.cambridgeday.com/2013/09/10/judith-ann-lippard/ |title=Judith Ann Lippard |publisher=Cambridge Day |date=2013-09-09 |access-date=2013-11-06}}</ref>  Stephen moved to Washington, DC, in 2017, where he remains active in science, writing, consulting, and grandfathering, while expanding his [[harpsichord]] playing and cooking skills.{{citation needed|date=September 2019}}
